title: South Africa | FAIS Fit and Proper, Treating Customers Fairly and Complaints
tagline: Learn the FSCA rules South African bank staff live by: fit and proper competence, CPD, fair treatment, complaints and speaking up.
sectors: Banks and their FAIS-authorised advice functions
Branches, contact centres and complaints teams
Bank compliance, conduct risk and learning functions
description:
This quest teaches the conduct rules that the **Financial Sector Conduct Authority (FSCA)** applies to South African banks and their staff. It covers the **FAIS Act** and the **Determination of Fit and Proper Requirements, 2017 (Board Notice 194 of 2017)**: honesty, integrity and good standing, competence, regulatory examinations, class of business and product specific training, the competence register and **continuous professional development**. It then explains the six **Treating Customers Fairly** outcomes, the **Conduct Standard for Banks (Conduct Standard 3 of 2020)** in general terms (its own text could not be opened, so details come from FSCA documents), complaints handling as assessed in the FSCA's **2025 banking complaints review**, the **Protected Disclosures Act** and **POPIA** confidentiality.

It is for bank staff appointed as FAIS representatives, their supervisors and key individuals, and the complaints, conduct and learning teams around them, because the bank must keep every representative fit and proper before and throughout their appointment.

You follow a fictional team at Amanzi Bank in Johannesburg, Cape Town, Durban, Gqeberha and Polokwane, and study real FSCA cases.

This quest builds knowledge of the law and good practice; it does not replace your institution's own policies, procedures or advice from your compliance team.
audience: Bank staff appointed as FAIS representatives for deposits, investments and other financial products
Key individuals, branch managers and team leaders who supervise representatives
Complaints, customer resolution and conduct risk teams
Learning and competence teams who keep the competence register and CPD records
Compliance, marketing and product staff who approve customer communications
outcomes: Explain who may render financial services at a bank under FAIS and the six fit and proper requirements in BN 194 of 2017
Apply the competence rules: experience, qualifications, regulatory exams and class and product training before rendering services
Manage CPD: the 1 June to 31 May cycle, minimum hours, accreditation, deadlines and records
Use the six TCF outcomes and the FSCA's findings on advertising and complaints to judge fair treatment
Handle protected disclosures and customer information in line with the Protected Disclosures Act and POPIA
Prepare honest evidence of competence and complaints handling for the FSCA

quest.name: The Green Tag Mission
quest.premise: You have just joined the conduct and FAIS compliance team at Amanzi Bank in Sandton. With conduct head Nandi Mthembu, competence lead Pieter van der Merwe, Durban branch manager Ayesha Patel, complaints lead Sipho Ndlovu and new consultant Lerato Mokoena, you must make sure everyone who wears the green REP tag is fit and proper, and that every customer is treated fairly from advert to complaint.

sessions.title: FAIS and the fit and proper gate
sessions.summary: Meet the FSCA and FAIS, learn who may give advice at a bank, the six fit and proper requirements of BN 194 of 2017 and the personal duty to disclose.
objectives: Explain the FSCA's conduct role and what FAIS regulates at a bank
Distinguish FSPs, key individuals and representatives, and factual information from advice
List the six fit and proper requirements and explain why they apply continuously
Apply the honesty, integrity and good standing rules, including the duty to disclose

cards.title: Stage one: the badge on the lanyard
cards.setting: Conduct and compliance floor, Amanzi Bank head office, Sandton, Johannesburg. 08:40.

lines.text: Your first morning at Amanzi Bank. Every consultant who walks past wears a lanyard with a small green tag: REP.
Welcome! I'm Nandi Mthembu, head of conduct and FAIS compliance. I'm also one of the bank's approved key individuals, so the FSCA knows my name.
Pieter van der Merwe, learning and competence, Cape Town. That green tag means the person is appointed as a FAIS representative. My job is proving each one is fit and proper.
Ayesha Patel, branch manager in Durban. Half my team has the tag, half doesn't. The ones without it keep asking why they can't just help customers choose a fixed deposit.
Sipho Ndlovu, complaints and customer resolution, Gqeberha. When someone without the tag gives advice anyway, the complaint lands on my desk.
Lerato Mokoena, new investment consultant in Polokwane. I start next month. I'd love to know what I must finish before my tag arrives!
Then that's your quest: five stages and a final exam. Stage one asks the big question. Who may give financial advice at a South African bank, and what does fit and proper really mean?

cards.title: FAIS in five scenes

scenes.heading: The conduct regulator
scenes.narration: The Financial Sector Conduct Authority, the FSCA, supervises how financial institutions, banks included, treat their customers. Under the Financial Sector Regulation Act, promoting the fair treatment of financial customers is part of its mandate.

scenes.heading: The FAIS Act
scenes.narration: The Financial Advisory and Intermediary Services Act of 2002, known as FAIS, regulates people and firms who give advice or intermediary services on financial products. Deposits, investments and insurance are all financial products under FAIS.

scenes.heading: The bank as an FSP
scenes.narration: A bank whose staff advise on or arrange financial products acts as an authorised financial services provider, or FSP. Its key individuals manage and oversee those services.

scenes.heading: Representatives
scenes.narration: Staff who give advice or intermediary services on the bank's behalf are appointed as representatives. Staff who are not appointed, or who do not meet the competence requirements, must not render financial services at all.

scenes.heading: Fit and proper, always
scenes.narration: The FSCA's Fit and Proper Determination, Board Notice 194 of 2017, sets the bar. It is not a test you pass once: FSPs, key individuals and representatives must keep meeting it for as long as they are authorised or appointed.

cards.title: The six fit and proper requirements

items.label: Honesty and integrity
items.detail: Personal character: truthful, trustworthy, no dishonest conduct.

items.label: Good standing
items.detail: No disqualifying history with courts, regulators or professional bodies.

items.label: Competence
items.detail: Experience, qualifications, exams and product training for the role.

items.label: Continuous professional development
items.detail: Keeping knowledge current through verifiable CPD each cycle.

items.label: Operational ability
items.detail: The FSP has the people, systems and governance to serve clients fairly.

items.label: Financial soundness
items.detail: The FSP is financially able to run its business.

cards.caption: Section 4 of Board Notice 194 of 2017 lists these six. Character sits at the top: no amount of training fixes a dishonest adviser.

cards.question: Lerato will advise customers on Amanzi Bank's fixed-term deposits. Under the FAIS framework, what is her status when she gives that advice?
options: A key individual of the bank
A representative of the bank as FSP
An independent FSP in her own right
An operator under POPIA
cards.explanation: Staff who render financial services on the bank's behalf are appointed as its representatives. Key individuals manage or oversee the services; Lerato will deliver them, so she needs to be appointed and fit and proper as a representative.

cards.title: Character first: honesty, integrity and good standing
cards.body:
Chapter 2 of the Determination applies to **every** FSP, key individual and representative. It lists events that point to a lack of honesty, integrity or good standing, for example:

- convictions for theft, fraud, forgery or other dishonesty, or under corruption laws
- civil findings of fraud, misrepresentation or breach of fiduciary duty
- being disciplined or removed by a regulator or professional body for honesty or business conduct reasons
- being untruthful with, or uncooperative towards, the regulator
- showing a lack of willingness to comply with legal or professional standards

The FSCA weighs the **seriousness** of the conduct, its **relevance** to the role and the **time** that has passed.

One duty sits with you personally: a representative must tell the FSP, **promptly, on their own initiative, fully and accurately**, anything that may affect their honesty, integrity or good standing.

cards.title: Fit and proper or red flag?
cards.prompt: Sort each fact about a candidate representative.
buckets: Red flag to disclose and assess

items.text: Completed product specific training on the bank's notice deposit before go-live
A civil judgment for misrepresentation to a former client
Debarred by the FSCA five years ago, never disclosed to the bank
Holds a qualification recognised for the products she will advise on
Gave a regulator a false answer during an earlier inspection
Logged verifiable, accredited CPD hours for the last cycle
Dismissed by a previous employer for falsifying client forms
Disclosed a minor traffic fine voluntarily on joining

cards.title: A turn: the question nobody asked
cards.setting: Ayesha's branch, Umhlanga, Durban. Lunch break.

lines.text: Nandi, quick one. A teller without the REP tag told a pensioner which notice deposit to choose. She meant well, the customer was confused.
Did she explain the features, or did she recommend one for him?
She said: 'At your age, take the 32-day one, it's best for you.'
That's a recommendation based on his circumstances. If he complains, I'll have to treat it as advice.
And the Determination is clear: staff who aren't appointed as representatives must not render financial services. What should the branch do now?

cards.title: The untagged teller
cards.situation: A teller at Amanzi Bank, not appointed as a FAIS representative, recommended a specific notice deposit to an elderly customer based on his age and needs. The customer has not complained, and the product is not unsuitable on its face. Ayesha asks you what to do.

choices.text: Log it as a conduct incident, have an appointed representative contact the customer to review his needs, coach the teller on the line between information and advice, and report the facts to compliance.
choices.outcome: This is the strongest response. The customer gets a proper advice process, the bank has a record, and compliance can check whether this is a pattern that needs a control, such as scripts or refresher training.

choices.text: Ignore it, because the product was not unsuitable and the customer is happy.
choices.outcome: A suitable outcome by luck does not make the process compliant. Unappointed staff rendered a financial service, and the bank has no record or fix to show the FSCA.

choices.text: Appoint the teller as a representative today so that the advice is covered retroactively.
choices.outcome: Appointment cannot be backdated to cure past advice, and she would need to meet the competence requirements, including product training, before rendering services.

choices.text: Tell the teller to stop talking to customers about deposits at all.
choices.outcome: Partly helpful, because it stops the immediate risk, but tellers can still give factual information. The customer's needs are left unreviewed and the incident is not recorded.

cards.title: Information versus advice at the counter

items.label: What it is
items.left: Facts about features, rates, terms and fees
items.right: A recommendation or guidance on what suits this customer

items.label: Example
items.left: This deposit needs 32 days' notice to withdraw
items.right: At your age, take the 32-day deposit

items.label: Who may do it
items.left: Trained staff, within the bank's scripts

items.label: Customer's needs
items.right: Needs, circumstances and capacity must be assessed

items.label: Record
items.right: Advice record kept under the bank's FAIS process

cards.caption: The line between the two is where most branch FAIS incidents start. Your bank's procedures set the exact boundary and scripts.

cards.title: FAIS vocabulary

cards.back: Financial services provider: a person or firm authorised under FAIS to render financial services. A bank that advises on products acts as one.
A person approved to manage or oversee the FSP's financial services. Key individuals carry their own fit and proper duties.
A person who renders financial services for an FSP. The FSP must make sure each one is fit and proper before and during appointment.
Under FAIS, advice or an intermediary service on a financial product, such as arranging or processing it for a client.
A bar on rendering financial services. The FSCA uses it against people who are not, or are no longer, fit and proper.
Fit and proper is continuous: a person who stops meeting the requirements may no longer act.

cards.question: A representative at Amanzi Bank is charged with fraud in a matter unrelated to her work. The case has not been decided. What does the Determination expect of her?
options: Nothing until she is convicted
Tell the FSCA directly, but not her employer
Disclose it to the bank promptly and on her own initiative
Resign her appointment immediately
cards.explanation: A representative must disclose to its FSP, promptly, fully and on her own initiative, any information that may be relevant to her honesty, integrity and good standing. A pending fraud charge clearly may be relevant; the bank then assesses it.

cards.title: Real case: honesty and integrity, Wood and Pillay (FSCA, 2026)
cards.body:
In August 2026 the FSCA debarred two former senior officials of the Regiments group of financial services providers for **18 years** each, barring them from rendering financial services or acting as key individuals.

The FSCA's investigation, which also considered findings of the Zondo (State Capture) Commission, found a pattern of conduct between 2009 and 2016 that fell short of the honesty, integrity and good governance expected of senior people. The evidence pointed to improper payment arrangements and unlawful revenue-sharing and procurement practices.

**The lesson for bank staff:** fit and proper is not only about exams. The honesty and integrity limb follows people across their careers, and a regulator can act years after the conduct took place.

cards.title: Real case: acting without authorisation, Geldenhuis (FSCA, 2023)
cards.body:
In December 2023 the FSCA announced it had debarred Jacobus Geldenhuis for **20 years** and imposed an administrative penalty of about **R143 million** on him.

He had offered to invest clients' money in shares, but neither he nor his company was an authorised FSP or a representative of one. The FSCA found he ran a Ponzi-type scheme, used client funds for his own benefit, contravened section 7(1) of the FAIS Act and conducted the business of a bank without registration, contrary to the Banks Act. The matter was also referred to the criminal authorities.

**The lesson:** authorisation and appointment are the gate. Customers are told to check that whoever advises them is authorised for that specific product, and your bank's REP tag is part of that promise.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: The FSCA regulates conduct; FAIS governs advice and intermediary services on financial products, including bank deposits and investments.
A bank that advises acts as an FSP; staff who render financial services must be appointed representatives who are fit and proper.
BN 194 of 2017 sets six requirements: honesty and integrity, good standing, competence, CPD, operational ability and financial soundness.
Fit and proper is ongoing, and representatives must disclose relevant information to the bank promptly and on their own initiative.
Unappointed staff, or staff who fall short of competence, must not render financial services.

cards.prompt: Think about your own role. Which conversations with customers come closest to the line between information and advice, and how would you know you had crossed it?

quiz.question: Which South African authority is the market conduct regulator that administers the FAIS fit and proper requirements?
options: The Financial Sector Conduct Authority (FSCA)
The Prudential Authority
The Financial Intelligence Centre
The National Credit Regulator
quiz.explanation: The FSCA is the conduct regulator and administers FAIS. The Prudential Authority supervises safety and soundness, the FIC is the AML authority and the NCR regulates credit providers.

quiz.question: Which instrument sets the current FAIS fit and proper requirements discussed in this quest?
options: Conduct Standard 3 of 2020
The Protected Disclosures Act
Board Notice 194 of 2017
Directive 1 of 2026
quiz.explanation: The Determination of Fit and Proper Requirements for FSPs, 2017, was published as Board Notice 194 of 2017. Conduct Standard 3 of 2020 covers banks' fair treatment of customers, not FAIS competence.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the six fit and proper requirements listed in BN 194 of 2017?
options: Operational ability
Financial soundness
Continuous professional development
Minimum sales targets
quiz.explanation: The six requirements are honesty and integrity, good standing, competence, CPD, operational ability and financial soundness. Sales targets are a business matter and can even create conflicts with fair treatment.

quiz.question: A Durban teller who is not an appointed representative tells a customer which deposit best suits his retirement plans. What is the main FAIS problem?
options: Unappointed staff rendered a financial service
The teller quoted an interest rate
The customer was over 60
The deposit had a notice period
quiz.explanation: Staff who are not appointed as representatives must not render financial services. Recommending a product for a customer's circumstances is advice; quoting a rate on its own is factual information.

quiz.question: When does a representative need to meet the fit and proper requirements?
options: Only at the time of appointment
Before appointment and at all times while appointed
Only when the FSCA inspects the bank
Only after a customer complaint
quiz.explanation: The Determination requires ongoing compliance: a person must meet the requirements to be appointed and must continue to meet them to remain appointed.

quiz.question: Pieter learns that a newly hired consultant was dismissed by a former employer for falsifying client forms, which she did not mention. Which fit and proper requirement is most directly in question?
options: Operational ability of the bank
Financial soundness of the bank
Honesty, integrity and good standing
Class of business training
quiz.explanation: Dishonest conduct and failure to disclose relevant information go to honesty, integrity and good standing. Operational ability and financial soundness concern the FSP itself.

quiz.question: In weighing a past incident against a person's honesty and integrity, which factors must the regulator consider under BN 194 of 2017?
options: Seniority, salary and length of service
Seriousness, relevance to the role and time passed
Sales results, client numbers and age
Media coverage, rank and nationality
quiz.explanation: Section 9(3) directs the regulator to weigh the seriousness of the conduct, its relevance to the duties of the role and the passage of time since it happened.

quiz.question: Lerato is summonsed in a civil claim alleging she misrepresented a product in a previous job. What should she do?
options: Wait until the court decides the claim
Tell only her line manager informally
Ask a colleague to tell compliance later
Tell Amanzi Bank promptly, fully and on her own initiative
quiz.explanation: A representative must disclose to its FSP, promptly and on its own initiative, fully and accurately, information that may be relevant to honesty, integrity and good standing. Waiting or informal hints do not meet that standard.

quiz.question: In the 2023 Geldenhuis matter, what did the FSCA find besides a breach of the FAIS Act?
options: He failed his regulatory examination
He missed his CPD hours
He also conducted the business of a bank unlawfully
He mislabelled complaints
quiz.explanation: The FSCA found he contravened FAIS section 7(1) by acting without authorisation and conducted the business of a bank in contravention of the Banks Act. He was debarred for 20 years and penalised about R143 million.

quiz.question: What did the FSCA's 2026 debarment of Wood and Pillay mainly turn on?
options: Failure to complete product training
Conduct inconsistent with honesty and integrity
Late CPD submissions
Poor complaints categorisation
quiz.explanation: The FSCA found a pattern of conduct, including improper payments and unlawful revenue-sharing and procurement practices, that adversely affected their honesty and integrity, and debarred both for 18 years.

sessions.title: Competence: experience, exams and product training
sessions.summary: Work through experience, recognised qualifications, regulatory exams, Tier 1 and Tier 2 products, and the class and product training that must come before advice.
objectives: Explain the general competence requirement and why minimums are not proof of competence
Apply the Tier 1 and Tier 2 distinction to bank deposits and structured deposits
Describe what class of business and product specific training cover and when they are due
Keep the competence register accurate and verify exam certificates

cards.title: Stage two: the competence register
cards.setting: Learning and competence hub, Amanzi Bank, Foreshore, Cape Town. 10:15.

lines.text: Welcome to my world: the competence register. Every representative has a row. Every row has to be provable.
Mine is half empty. Qualification: yes. Experience: some. Regulatory exam: booked. Product training: not yet.
And until the right boxes are ticked for the products you'll handle, you don't advise on them. Even if you're brilliant.
Pieter, my branch wants to launch the new structured deposit next week. Do my deposit consultants need anything extra for that?
Very much so. A plain fixed deposit and a structured deposit sit in different tiers. Let's walk through why.
Stage two is about competence: experience, qualifications, exams and the training that must happen before the first conversation, not after.

cards.title: Competence, piece by piece

scenes.heading: The general test
scenes.narration: Every FSP, key individual and representative must have adequate, appropriate and relevant skills, knowledge and expertise for the services, products and functions they perform, and must keep that competence up to date.

scenes.heading: Experience
scenes.narration: Minimum experience applies per product and per type of service. For example, a Category I representative advising on short-term or long-term deposits needs at least six months' experience, and experience lapses after five years of not rendering that service.

scenes.heading: Qualifications
scenes.narration: People must hold a qualification the regulator recognises for their role. A narrow exception exists for staff who only execute scripted sales under strict controls and never give advice.

scenes.heading: Regulatory examinations
scenes.narration: Where they apply, the regulatory examinations must be passed before appointment. Representatives write the representatives' exam, known as RE 5; key individuals write RE 1.

scenes.heading: Class and product training
scenes.narration: Before rendering any financial service on a product, an FSP and its representatives must complete the class of business training and the product specific training for it.

cards.title: Tier 1 and Tier 2: why the deposit type matters

items.label: Regulatory exam (RE 5)
items.right: Not required if only Tier 2 products

items.label: Class of business training
items.right: Not required if only Tier 2 products

items.label: CPD
items.right: Not required if only Tier 2 products

cards.caption: Annexure Three of BN 194 lists Tier 1 and Tier 2 products. A structured deposit links its return to another product, asset, rate or index, so it is a Tier 1 product. Always check the current Determination.

cards.question: Ayesha's consultants are appointed only for ordinary fixed deposits. The bank now wants them to advise on a structured deposit whose return depends on a share index. What changes?
options: Nothing, because a deposit is always a Tier 2 product
They only need to sign the new product brochure
They need the Tier 1 requirements, including RE and training, first
They need a new branch manager to supervise them
cards.explanation: A structured deposit is a Tier 1 product in Annexure Three. Representatives must meet the Tier 1 competence requirements, including class of business and product specific training and the regulatory examination where it applies, before advising on it.

cards.title: What class and product training must cover
cards.body:
Section 29 of the Determination says training must happen **before** a person renders a financial service on a product, and lists what it should include where appropriate.

**Class of business training** covers the whole class: the range of products, typical features, fees and costs, general risks, which products suit which types of client, the role players, relevant law and tax, economic factors such as inflation and interest rates, and industry codes.

**Product specific training** goes deep on one product: its features and complexity, how it is structured and priced, fees and their effect on real returns, guarantees, risks, liquidity and access to funds, lock-ins and exit costs, the **target market and customers it does not suit**, required disclosures and the outcomes it should deliver for clients.

The FSP must record the training in its **competence register within 15 days** and keep the records for at least **five years** after the person stops rendering services on that product.

cards.title: Match the competence element to its rule
cards.prompt: Link each element to what BN 194 of 2017 says about it.

pairs.right: Set per product and service; lapses after five consecutive years of not rendering it
Must be recognised by the regulator for the role, with a narrow scripted-sales exception
Where it applies, must be passed before authorisation, approval or appointment
Completed before the first financial service on that product
Records qualifications, exams, training and CPD of everyone in scope
Entered in the register within 15 days of the training

cards.title: A turn: the certificate on WhatsApp
cards.setting: Video call between Cape Town and Polokwane. Late afternoon.

lines.text: Pieter, someone in a WhatsApp group is selling RE certificates. 'No studying, instant pass.' A new colleague asked me if it's legit.
It isn't. The FSCA has warned the public about forged regulatory examination certificates being sold on social media.
And think of the bank's side. If we accept a forged certificate, our competence register is false and the person isn't fit and proper.
So how do we check? I can't tell a real certificate from a good fake.
You don't guess. You verify with the examination body directly. That goes in our onboarding checklist today.

cards.title: The suspiciously quick RE pass
cards.situation: A recruit for Amanzi Bank's investment desk hands Pieter an RE 5 certificate dated two days after she was told to book the exam. The logo looks slightly off. Her start date is Monday and the business is short-staffed.

choices.text: Verify the certificate directly with the recognised examination body before appointment, keep her off advice until it is confirmed, and escalate to compliance if it proves false.
choices.outcome: Correct. The exam must be passed before appointment, and the bank must be able to prove it. Direct verification protects customers and the integrity of the register, and a forgery is a serious honesty matter.

choices.text: Appoint her on Monday and verify the certificate within the first month.
choices.outcome: Appointment before the exam is proven puts an unverified person in front of customers and records a possibly false fact in the register.

choices.text: Ask her to sign a declaration that the certificate is genuine and appoint her.
choices.outcome: A declaration helps the paper trail but does not verify anything. If the certificate is forged, the bank has still appointed someone who has not passed.

choices.text: Reject her application without telling her why.
choices.outcome: Unfair and premature. The right step is to verify; if the certificate is genuine she should proceed, and if it is not, the matter is handled through a proper process.

cards.title: From hire to first advice conversation

items.label: Fit and proper screening
items.detail: Honesty, integrity and good standing checks and disclosures.

items.label: Qualification and experience
items.detail: Confirm a recognised qualification and the experience the role needs.

items.label: Regulatory examination
items.detail: Where it applies, verified pass before appointment.

items.label: Class and product training
items.detail: Completed for each product before rendering services.

items.label: Appointment and register
items.detail: Representative appointed; register updated within the set time.

items.label: Supervised start and review
items.detail: Monitoring and regular competence reviews from day one.

cards.caption: Your bank's onboarding process will add its own steps, such as debarment and credit checks and system access controls.

cards.title: Myth or fact?

cards.front: Myth: a bank deposit is too simple to need any training.
cards.back: Fact: even for Tier 2 deposits, product specific training is still required before the representative renders services on them.

cards.front: Myth: passing the exam proves a person is competent.
cards.back: Fact: the Determination says the minimum requirements alone do not prove competence. The FSP must still assess skills, knowledge and expertise.
Fact: experience for a product and service lapses after five consecutive years of not rendering it.

cards.front: Myth: product training can happen in the first month on the job.
cards.back: Fact: it must be completed before the first financial service on that product.

cards.front: Myth: suitability is the compliance team's job.
cards.back: Fact: the FSP must make sure representatives can judge whether a product suits a client's needs, circumstances, risk tolerance and understanding.

cards.question: Which of these does the Determination expect representatives to be able to do, as part of the FSP's competence responsibilities?
options: Guarantee a client's investment returns
Judge whether a product suits a client's needs and capacity
Approve their own appointment in the register
Set the product's fees and charges
cards.explanation: Section 13(1)(f) requires the FSP to ensure its people can assess whether a service or product is appropriate, given the client's needs, circumstances, risk tolerance and capacity to understand its features and complexity.

cards.title: Real case: forged exam certificates (FSCA warning, 2023)
cards.body:
In December 2023 the FSCA warned the public that individuals were selling **fraudulent regulatory examination certificates** on social media, using the name and logo of a training company and of the FSCA itself. The forgeries closely resembled a genuine e-learning certificate.

The FSCA told candidates to deal directly with the examination body it had approved at the time, and invited employers to **verify certificates directly** with that body.

**The lesson for banks:** the regulatory examination is a gate to appointment. An FSP that accepts certificates without checking them risks appointing people who have not passed, and a buyer of a fake certificate raises a serious honesty and integrity question.

cards.title: Real case: advising beyond the licence, Warriner (FSCA, 2024)
cards.body:
In May 2024 the FSCA debarred Craig Warriner for **30 years**. Its investigation found that he and a trust had exercised discretion in buying and selling securities for clients, which required authorisation as a discretionary (Category II) FSP that they did not have, and that he rendered financial services on behalf of an unauthorised entity.

The debarment bars him from providing financial services, acting as a key person of a financial institution and providing specified services to one, including through outsourcing.

In its warnings the FSCA tells the public to check **which category and products** an adviser is authorised for, because some people registered for simple, low-risk products go on to advise on complex, risky ones.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: Competence means adequate, appropriate and relevant skills, knowledge and expertise for the products and services you handle, kept current.
Experience, recognised qualifications and, where they apply, regulatory exams are minimums, not proof of competence on their own.
Class of business and product specific training must be completed before you render a service on a product; Tier 2 deposits still need product training.
A structured deposit is a Tier 1 product, so the stricter requirements apply before advising on it.
The bank keeps a competence register and must be able to prove every entry, including verified exam passes.

cards.prompt: Pick one product you deal with. Could you explain its fees, risks, access to funds and the customers it does not suit without looking anything up? Where are your gaps?

quiz.question: Under BN 194 of 2017, when must a representative complete product specific training for a financial product?
options: Within the first three months of appointment
Only after the first customer complaint
Before rendering any financial service on it
At the end of the first CPD cycle
quiz.explanation: Section 29(1) requires class of business and product specific training to be completed before the person renders any financial service in respect of that product.

quiz.question: In Annexure Three of BN 194 of 2017, how is a structured deposit classified?
options: As a Tier 1 financial product
As a Tier 2 financial product
As a non-financial product
As a short-term insurance product
quiz.explanation: Structured deposits are listed as Tier 1 products, while short-term and long-term deposits are Tier 2. The structured deposit's return depends on another product, asset, rate or index.

quiz.question: A Polokwane consultant is appointed only to advise on short-term and long-term deposits (Tier 2). Which requirement still applies to her?
options: The RE 5 regulatory examination
Class of business training
The annual CPD hours
Product specific training on those deposits
quiz.explanation: Representatives who only render services on Tier 2 products are exempt from the regulatory exam, class of business training and CPD, but the product specific training requirement still applies.

quiz.question: Within what period must the FSP record a representative's product specific or class of business training in its competence register?
options: Within 30 days after the CPD cycle
Within 15 days after the training
Within 6 months of appointment
Before the next FSCA inspection
quiz.explanation: Section 30(a) requires the FSP to record the training in the competence register within 15 days after it has occurred. The 30-day period applies to recording CPD after each cycle.

quiz.question: Pieter says: 'She passed RE 5 and has her qualification, so she is competent.' What does BN 194 of 2017 say about that view?
options: It is correct for Tier 1 products
It is correct if she has CPD too
Minimums alone do not prove competence
It is correct once she is appointed
quiz.explanation: Section 13(8) states that meeting the minimum requirements does not in itself show that a person meets the general competence requirement of adequate, appropriate and relevant skills, knowledge and expertise.

quiz.question: A recruit's regulatory exam certificate looks forged. When must the exam, where it applies, have been passed?
options: Before her appointment as a representative
Within a year of appointment
Before her first CPD cycle ends
Before her first customer complaint
quiz.explanation: Section 26(6) requires the applicable regulatory examinations to be passed before authorisation, approval or appointment, so the bank must verify the pass before appointing her.

quiz.question: Which topic belongs in product specific training rather than in general class of business training?
options: The range of products within the whole class
Customers for whom this product is not expected to be suitable
General role players in the market
Economic cycles affecting the class
quiz.explanation: Product specific training covers the product's target market and the customers it does not suit, along with its structure, fees and risks. The other topics describe class of business training.

quiz.question: A representative stopped advising on deposits six years ago and has not done so since. What happens to that experience under BN 194 of 2017?
options: It stays valid for the rest of her career
It lapses only if she changes employer
It lapses after ten consecutive years
It has lapsed after five consecutive years
quiz.explanation: Section 16 provides that experience lapses when the person has not rendered the particular financial service on that product for five consecutive years.

quiz.question: Which responsibility does section 13(1) of BN 194 of 2017 place on the FSP regarding staff who are not appointed as representatives?
options: Make sure they do not render financial services
Register them with the FSCA as trainees
Enrol them in CPD every cycle
Let them advise under a manager's name
quiz.explanation: Section 13(1)(g) requires the FSP's controls to ensure that people who do not meet the competency requirements, and staff who are not appointed as representatives, do not render financial services.

quiz.question: In its 2024 Warriner press release, what did the FSCA urge the public to check besides authorisation?
options: The adviser's social media following
The adviser's years at university
The category and products the adviser is licensed for
The adviser's sales awards
quiz.explanation: The FSCA urged people to check what category of advice someone is registered for, because some people registered for basic, low-risk products go on to advise on complex ones.

sessions.title: CPD and staying competent
sessions.summary: Learn the CPD cycle, minimum hours, what counts, deadlines and records, reductions for long absences and how to verify CPD providers.
objectives: Calculate CPD hours, including pro rata for part-year appointments
Decide whether an activity counts as accredited, verifiable CPD
Apply the 15-day, 30-day and five-year record rules
Explain how the bank regularly reviews competence and verifies providers

cards.title: Stage three: the 31 May scramble
cards.setting: Learning and competence hub, Cape Town. Late May.

lines.text: It's that time of year. The CPD cycle closes on 31 May, and I have forty representatives with missing hours.
I joined in January. Do I owe a full year of hours, or only part?
And one of my consultants just sent me a CPD certificate from a provider I've never heard of. Ten hours, done in one evening.
Two good questions. CPD is not a box-ticking race. It has to be accredited, verifiable and relevant to the work you actually do.
Relevant matters to me too. Half my complaints come from consultants who know the old product rules, not the new ones.
Stage three: staying competent. CPD hours, the cycle, the records, and how the bank checks that people are still good at their jobs.

cards.title: How CPD works under FAIS

scenes.heading: A yearly cycle
scenes.narration: Under BN 194 of 2017, a CPD cycle runs for twelve months, from 1 June each year to 31 May the next. Hours are counted per cycle.

scenes.heading: Relevant learning
scenes.narration: CPD activities must fit the person's role, build skill, knowledge and professional and ethical standards, and close identified gaps, including gaps in knowledge of the law.

scenes.heading: Accredited and verifiable
scenes.narration: A CPD activity is accredited by a professional body, carries an hour value from that body, and can be objectively verified, including who took part and proof of completion.

scenes.heading: What does not count
scenes.narration: Work towards a qualification and product specific training are excluded from the definition of CPD activity. They are separate requirements.

scenes.heading: Plans and records
scenes.narration: The FSP needs CPD policies and a training plan for each cycle, and must record, calculate and keep evidence of everyone's CPD.

cards.title: Minimum CPD hours per cycle

items.label: One subclass, one class
items.detail: A single subclass of business within one class of business.

items.label: Several subclasses, one class
items.detail: More than one subclass within a single class of business.

items.label: More than one class
items.detail: Authorised or appointed across more than one class of business.

items.label: Part-year appointment
items.detail: Hours pro-rated by the months appointed in that cycle.

cards.caption: Section 33 of BN 194 of 2017. Representatives who only render services on Tier 2 products, such as ordinary deposits, are outside the CPD chapter. Check the current Determination for any changes.

cards.question: Lerato was appointed on 1 January to advise on more than one class of business. Her full-year requirement would be 18 hours. Roughly how many CPD hours must she complete by 31 May?
options: 18 hours, because the minimum is never reduced
About 7.5 hours, pro-rated for five months
None, because new staff are exempt in their first cycle
About 1.5 hours, one per month
cards.explanation: For part-year appointments, the hours are pro-rated: the annual hours divided by 12, multiplied by the months appointed in the cycle. 18 ÷ 12 × 5 = 7.5 hours.

cards.title: Deadlines and evidence in the CPD chapter
cards.body:
BN 194 of 2017 builds a clear evidence trail:

- Representatives and key individuals **submit CPD evidence to the FSP within 15 days** after the cycle ends.
- The FSP **records** everyone's CPD in the competence register **within 30 days** after the cycle ends, calculates each person's total hours and keeps supporting evidence.
- Evidence is **kept for at least five years** from the end of the cycle.

The FSP may **reduce** a representative's hours pro rata for a continuous absence due to maternity, paternity or adoption leave, long-term illness or disability, or caring for a family member with a long-term illness or disability. It must record the dates, reasons and evidence. Reductions do not roll over into the next cycle unless the same absence continues, and never for more than **three consecutive cycles**.

Separately, the FSP must **regularly evaluate and review** each person's competence and the appropriateness of its training and CPD, looking at technical knowledge, skills and changes in products, markets and law.

cards.title: Counts as CPD or not?
cards.prompt: Sort each activity for a representative who must earn CPD hours.

items.text: An accredited webinar on changes to tax rules, with an hour value and attendance proof
Modules completed towards a degree she is studying for
Product specific training on the bank's new structured deposit
An accredited ethics workshop with a verified completion certificate
A ten-hour certificate from a provider whose accreditation number is invalid
Reading the newspaper's business pages over the weekend
An accredited course on retirement products, logged with the professional body
A team lunch where colleagues discussed market trends

cards.title: A turn: the one-evening certificate

lines.text: The provider calls itself a CPD house and the certificate carries a professional body's logo. It looks official.
The FSCA warned about exactly this in 2025: a company issuing CPD certificates with a professional body's logo and reference numbers that were invalid or belonged to others.
And the FSCA said that failing to verify providers can leave the institution itself short of its CPD requirements.
So my consultant could be short of hours without knowing it. And the register would be wrong.
Which is why we verify the provider and the accreditation with the professional body before anyone books.

cards.title: Hours that don't add up
cards.situation: On 10 June, an investment consultant at Amanzi Bank submits CPD evidence for the cycle that ended on 31 May. Six of her twelve required hours come from a provider whose accreditation reference the professional body says belongs to someone else. She says she did not know.

choices.text: Do not record the six hours, explain why, agree a plan for her to make good the shortfall with verified activities, assess her competence and any limits on her advice, and report the provider and the gap through compliance.
choices.outcome: Best answer. The register must only show verifiable, accredited CPD. The bank deals fairly with the consultant, manages the risk to customers, and fixes the control weakness that let an unverified provider through.

choices.text: Record all twelve hours, since she acted in good faith.
choices.outcome: Good faith does not make the hours accredited or verifiable. The register would contain a false entry and the bank could not show compliance.

choices.text: Record the six valid hours and leave the matter there.
choices.outcome: The record is accurate, which is a start, but the shortfall, the competence review and the provider problem are ignored.

choices.text: Suspend her immediately and start a disciplinary hearing for dishonesty.
choices.outcome: Too quick. There is no evidence she knew. The right path is to correct the record and assess the facts before deciding on any further action.

cards.title: The CPD year at Amanzi Bank

items.label: CPD cycle opens
items.detail: New 12-month cycle; training plan for the cycle in place.

items.label: Mid-cycle check
items.detail: Learning team flags people behind plan and gaps from reviews.

items.label: Cycle closes
items.detail: Last day for hours to count in this cycle.

items.label: Evidence due from staff
items.detail: Representatives submit CPD evidence to the bank.

items.label: Register updated
items.detail: Bank records CPD and calculates totals per person.

items.label: Records kept
items.detail: Supporting evidence retained from the end of the cycle.

cards.caption: The dates and periods come from BN 194 of 2017; the December check is Amanzi Bank's own good practice.

cards.title: Verify a new CPD provider
cards.prompt: Put the steps in the order a careful learning team would follow.
steps: Identify the learning need from competence reviews or law changes
Shortlist providers and ask for accreditation details and hour values
Verify the accreditation directly with the professional body
Approve the provider and the activity in the CPD plan
Collect verifiable completion evidence after the activity
Record the hours in the competence register on time

cards.question: Which of these is a ground on which the bank may reduce a representative's CPD hours pro rata under BN 194 of 2017?
options: A heavy sales month
A change of branch
A long-term illness absence
A promotion to team leader
cards.explanation: Section 34 allows a pro rata reduction for continuous absence due to maternity, paternity or adoption leave, long-term illness or disability, or caring for a family member with a long-term illness or disability. Workload and job moves are not grounds.

cards.title: Real case: an unverified CPD provider (FSCA warning, 2025)
cards.body:
In June 2025 the FSCA warned that a company called **LearnOn** had been offering CPD services to FSPs without the necessary authorisation. It said LearnOn appeared to have issued CPD certificates bearing the logo of the Financial Planning Institute of South Africa without permission, using reference numbers that were invalid or belonged to other approved providers.

The FSCA did not comment on the content of the courses. Its message was about **verification**: institutions should check the accreditation of CPD providers with the relevant professional body before signing up, because failing to do so may leave them short of the CPD requirements in BN 194 of 2017.

**The lesson:** the CPD record is the bank's evidence. It is only as good as the accreditation behind it.

cards.title: Real case: training as the fix (FSCA banking complaints review, 2025)
cards.body:
The FSCA's 2025 report on complaints management in banks shows how training and quality checks keep competence alive. After the review, one of the four major banks found that a complaints system needing daily input from many employees produced inconsistent results. It **improved employee training**, updated its procedures manual and quality assurance checklist, and began **periodic spot checks**.

The report also recorded that banks generally developed and implemented training interventions to put their complaints frameworks into practice. The FSCA said it would keep monitoring, including whether **proper employee training** was in place.

**The lesson:** competence is maintained, not assumed. Spot checks and targeted refreshers are how a bank proves people are still doing the job right.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: The CPD cycle runs from 1 June to 31 May; minimum hours are 6, 12 or 18 depending on the classes and subclasses of business.
CPD must be accredited by a professional body, carry an hour value and be verifiable; qualification work and product training do not count.
Staff submit evidence within 15 days of the cycle's end; the bank records it within 30 days and keeps evidence for five years.
Hours are pro-rated for part-year appointments and may be reduced only for the listed long absences, within strict limits.
The bank must regularly review competence and the fitness of its training, and verify CPD providers before using them.

cards.prompt: Look at your last year of learning. Which activities were accredited and verifiable, and which were useful but would not count? What one gap should your next CPD activity close?

quiz.question: Under BN 194 of 2017, when does a CPD cycle run?
options: From 1 January to 31 December
From 1 June to 31 May of the next year
From 1 April to 31 March of the next year
From each person's appointment anniversary
quiz.explanation: The Determination defines the CPD cycle as twelve months starting on 1 June and ending on 31 May of the following year.

quiz.question: A representative is appointed for more than one class of business for a full cycle. What is the minimum CPD requirement?
options: 6 hours per cycle
12 hours per cycle
24 hours per cycle
18 hours per cycle
quiz.explanation: Section 33(1)(c) sets 18 hours for more than one class of business. Six hours applies to a single subclass and twelve to several subclasses within one class.

quiz.question: Which activity is excluded from the definition of a CPD activity?
options: Product specific training
An accredited ethics course
An accredited tax update webinar
An accredited compliance workshop
quiz.explanation: The definition excludes activities towards a qualification and product specific training. Accredited, hour-rated and verifiable activities such as the others can count.

quiz.question: Within what period after a CPD cycle ends must representatives submit their CPD evidence to the FSP?
options: Within 7 days
Within 60 days
Within 15 days
Within 90 days
quiz.explanation: Section 33(2) requires key individuals and representatives to submit evidence of CPD activities to the FSP within 15 days after the cycle ends; the FSP then records it within 30 days.

quiz.question: For how long must the FSP keep supporting evidence of recorded CPD activities?
options: One year from the end of the cycle
At least five years from the end of the cycle
Until the person leaves the bank
Until the next FSCA inspection
quiz.explanation: Section 32(3)(e) requires the evidence to be retained for not less than five years from the end of the CPD cycle concerned.

quiz.question: A Gqeberha consultant is on maternity leave for four months of a cycle. What may the bank do about her CPD hours?
options: Cancel her CPD requirement for that cycle
Double her hours in the following cycle
Leave the full requirement unchanged by law
Reduce them pro rata and record the reason and evidence
quiz.explanation: Section 34 allows a pro rata reduction for continuous absence on maternity leave; section 32(3)(d) requires the dates, reasons and supporting evidence of the decision to be recorded.

quiz.question: A representative is absent with a long-term illness that starts in one cycle and continues unbroken. For how many consecutive cycles at most may the reduction apply?
options: Three consecutive cycles
One cycle only
Two consecutive cycles
As many cycles as the illness lasts
quiz.explanation: Reductions cannot normally run across consecutive cycles, except where the absence continues without a break, and then only for a maximum of three consecutive CPD cycles.

quiz.question: In 2025 the FSCA warned financial institutions about LearnOn. What was its main message?
options: Stop all online CPD courses
Only use the FSCA's own courses
Verify CPD providers' accreditation before using them
Report CPD hours directly to the FSCA
quiz.explanation: The FSCA urged institutions to verify the accreditation of CPD providers with the relevant professional bodies, warning that unverified providers could leave them short of the BN 194 CPD requirements.

quiz.question: Which factors must the FSP take into account when it regularly evaluates a representative's competence under section 13 of BN 194 of 2017?
options: Sales volumes, branch rankings and bonuses
Technical knowledge, skills and changes in products and law
Length of service, age and seniority
Customer satisfaction scores only
quiz.explanation: Section 13(4) lists technical knowledge and its application, skills and expertise, and changes in the market, products, services and legislation.

quiz.question: A consultant appointed only for ordinary short-term and long-term deposits asks whether she needs CPD hours. What is the answer under BN 194 of 2017?
options: No, Tier 2-only representatives fall outside the CPD chapter
Yes, 6 hours, because deposits are one subclass
Yes, 18 hours, because deposits span two classes
Only if she has worked there for a year
quiz.explanation: Section 31(2)(b)(i) excludes representatives appointed only to render financial services on Tier 2 products, and ordinary deposits are Tier 2. The bank may still require learning under its own policy.

sessions.title: Treating customers fairly and complaints
sessions.summary: Apply the six TCF outcomes, the Conduct Standard for Banks as the FSCA describes it, the African Bank advertising case and the FSCA's 2025 banking complaints review.
objectives: Explain the six TCF outcomes and link failures to them
Recognise misleading advertising and the need for an approval process
Handle a complaint the way the section 8 requirements assessed by the FSCA expect
Use the FSCA's 2025 review findings to spot weak complaints practice

cards.title: Stage four: the complaints register
cards.setting: Customer resolution centre, Amanzi Bank, Gqeberha. 09:00.

lines.text: Morning! This is the complaints register. Every row is a customer who felt let down. My problem: I can't tell how many we upheld, or how many we sent to the ombud.
That's exactly what the FSCA found across the industry when it reviewed bank complaints. Weak records, weak categories, customers left in the dark.
And complaints are only the end of the story, right? The start is how we design, advertise and sell products.
Our marketing team wants a festive loan campaign with a celebrity. 'Treat yourself, it's an investment in you.' Is that a problem?
It might be a very expensive one. The FSCA fined a bank in 2025 for a loan advert that dressed credit up as an investment.
Stage four: treating customers fairly. The six outcomes, the Conduct Standard for Banks, and complaints done properly.

cards.title: Fair treatment in South African banking

scenes.heading: A legal mandate
scenes.narration: The Financial Sector Regulation Act gives the FSCA the objective of protecting financial customers, including by promoting their fair treatment by financial institutions.

scenes.heading: The TCF outcomes
scenes.narration: Since 2011 the regulator has described fair treatment through six Treating Customers Fairly outcomes, often called TCF. They cover culture, product design, information, advice, product performance and post-sale barriers.

scenes.heading: A standard for banks
scenes.narration: For banks, the FSCA made Conduct Standard 3 of 2020, the Conduct Standard for Banks. According to the FSCA, it took effect in July 2021 and sets requirements for banks' fair treatment of customers.

scenes.heading: Advertising rules
scenes.narration: The FSCA has described the standard's advertising rules: adverts must be clear, fair and not misleading, factually correct, and approved through a process involving a person of appropriate seniority and expertise.

scenes.heading: Complaints rules
scenes.narration: Section 8 of the standard deals with complaints: categorising them, recording them, acknowledging them, keeping complainants informed, giving reasons, and telling customers about the ombud.

cards.title: The six TCF outcomes along the customer journey

items.label: 1. Fair culture
items.detail: Fair treatment is built into the bank's culture and leadership.

items.label: 2. Right product design
items.detail: Products meet the needs of the customers they target, and are marketed to them.

items.label: 3. Clear information
items.detail: Customers are kept appropriately informed before, during and after the sale.

items.label: 4. Suitable advice
items.detail: Where advice is given, it suits the customer's needs and circumstances.

items.label: 5. Performs as promised
items.detail: Products perform as customers were led to expect, with adequate service.

items.label: 6. No unreasonable barriers
items.detail: Customers can change, claim, complain or leave without unfair obstacles.

cards.caption: Paraphrased from the FSCA's description of the six outcomes in its study of financial customer behaviour and sentiment.

cards.question: Amanzi Bank's fixed deposit brochure hides an early-withdrawal penalty in tiny print on the last page. Which TCF outcome is most directly at risk?
options: Outcome 1: fair culture
Outcome 4: suitable advice
Outcome 3: clear information
Outcome 6: post-sale barriers
cards.explanation: Outcome 3 expects customers to get clear information and be kept appropriately informed before, during and after the sale. A hidden penalty also creates a later barrier, but the first failure is in the information.

cards.title: A note on the Conduct Standard for Banks
cards.body:
This quest could not open the official text of **Conduct Standard 3 of 2020 (Banks)**, so its detail is kept general. What we know comes from FSCA documents that were opened:

- The FSCA says the standard became effective in **July 2021** and sets requirements for banks' fair treatment of financial customers.
- In a 2025 enforcement case the FSCA described **section 6** as requiring adverts that are clear, fair and not misleading, factually correct and free of untrue or misleading statements, with an **approval process** involving a person of appropriate seniority and expertise.
- The FSCA's 2025 complaints review assessed banks against parts of **section 8**: categorising complaints in minimum categories, keeping accurate and secure complaint records and data, acknowledging complaints and explaining the process, keeping complainants informed about progress and delays, giving clear reasons for rejections and the escalation options, and telling customers how to reach the **relevant ombud** at all relevant stages.

For exact wording and timelines, read the current standard on the FSCA website and follow your bank's complaints policy.

cards.title: Match the complaints duty to the gap the FSCA found
cards.prompt: Link each part of section 8 assessed in the FSCA's 2025 banking review to the weakness it reported.

pairs.right: Some banks still sorted complaints by the old TCF headings, not the standard's categories
Registers lacked key documents, decisions and whether timelines were met
Registers did not show upheld or rejected, ombud referrals or goodwill paid
No evidence complainants got the handler's contact details or indicative timelines
Customers not told about progress, causes of delay or revised timelines
Ombud availability not shared throughout the product life cycle

cards.title: A turn: the festive campaign

lines.text: Here's the draft: a famous comedian holding cash, and the line 'This loan isn't debt, it's an investment in your best December ever.'
I can already see the complaints in March when the repayments bite.
A loan isn't an investment. Customers could misunderstand the cost and the risk.
That's almost exactly what the FSCA penalised in 2025. And it also criticised the bank's approval process for letting the advert through.
Marketing says the campaign goes live on Friday. What do we do?

cards.title: The 'loan as investment' advert
cards.situation: Amanzi Bank's marketing team plans a social media campaign for personal loans that calls the loan 'an investment in you'. Launch is in three days. The advert has not been through the bank's conduct approval step.

choices.text: Stop the launch until the advert goes through the bank's approval process with a suitably senior, expert reviewer, and rewrite it so it is factually correct and clearly presents the product as credit with its costs.
choices.outcome: Right. The FSCA's reading of the Conduct Standard requires clear, fair, factually correct adverts and a governance process for approval. Fixing it before launch protects customers and the bank.

choices.text: Launch on time but add 'terms and conditions apply' in small print.
choices.outcome: Small print does not cure a misleading headline. Customers would still be misled about the nature of the product.

choices.text: Launch, then monitor social media for complaints and pull the advert if many arrive.
choices.outcome: Waiting for harm reverses the logic of fair treatment. The advert would already have misled customers, and the approval failure would remain.

choices.text: Change 'investment' to 'treat' and launch without further review.
choices.outcome: Better wording, but skipping the approval process repeats the governance weakness the FSCA criticised, and other claims may still mislead.

cards.title: A complaint handled the way section 8 expects

items.label: Receive and record
items.detail: Capture the complaint accurately and securely, with all documents.

items.label: Categorise
items.detail: Use the minimum categories so data and root causes are reliable.

items.label: Acknowledge
items.detail: Confirm receipt, the handler's contact details and the process.

items.label: Keep informed
items.detail: Update on progress, delays and revised timelines.

items.label: Decide and explain
items.detail: Give the outcome; if rejected, clear reasons and escalation options.

items.label: Point to the ombud
items.detail: Give the relevant ombud's details, as at other relevant stages.

cards.caption: Built from the requirements the FSCA assessed in its 2025 review. Your bank's policy sets the exact timelines and templates.

cards.title: TCF myths and facts

cards.front: Myth: TCF only matters at the point of sale.
cards.back: Fact: the outcomes run from culture and product design to after-sale service, complaints and switching.

cards.front: Myth: if a complaint is resolved, nothing else needs recording.
cards.back: Fact: the FSCA found banks failing to record whether complaints were upheld or rejected, ombud referrals, and goodwill payments.

cards.front: Myth: a rejected complaint just needs a polite 'no'.
cards.back: Fact: customers should get clear reasons and details of any escalation or review process and how to use it.

cards.front: Myth: ombud details only go in the final letter.
cards.back: Fact: the FSCA expects them at all relevant stages, including point of sale and periodic communications.

cards.front: Myth: fraud complaints should be sent to the police instead.
cards.back: Fact: the FSCA criticised banks that referred complainants to the police rather than giving them the relevant ombud's details.

cards.question: In the FSCA's 2025 banking complaints review, which weakness affected the largest share of banks?
options: Failing to categorise complaints
Failing to keep complainants informed of progress
Failing to keep data by category
Failing to give ombud details
cards.explanation: 92% of banks did not adequately keep complainants informed of progress, delays and decisions. The other weaknesses affected 60% to 85% of banks.

cards.title: Real case: misleading loan advert, African Bank (FSCA, 2025)
cards.body:
In April 2025 the FSCA imposed an administrative penalty of **R700 000** on African Bank for a December 2023 social media campaign for personal loans. The advert, featuring a well-known public figure, suggested the loan was an investment rather than credit.

The FSCA found the statement factually incorrect and misleading, in breach of section 6 of the Conduct Standard for Banks, and found weaknesses in the bank's **governance and approval** of the advert. Because the bank cooperated and fixed the issues promptly, **R200 000** of the penalty was suspended for two years on condition of continued compliance; the bank paid **R500 000**.

**The lesson:** customers choose products based on what adverts tell them. Calling credit an investment hides the cost and risk, and every bank needs a real approval gate.

cards.title: Real case: the FSCA's banking complaints review (2025)
cards.body:
The FSCA ran a desktop review between July and November 2022 and published it in **February 2025**. Twenty-three banks submitted complaints registers covering July 2021 to June 2022, with **316 133** complaints in total; the FSCA sampled up to 100 per bank.

It found that **none** of the sampled banks satisfied all of the section 8 requirements assessed. Problems included complaints not categorised as the standard requires, registers that did not show whether complaints were upheld, missing records of goodwill payments, no proof that complainants got the handler's contact details or timelines, and some customers being sent to the police rather than told about the relevant ombud.

The FSCA also noted good practice after the review: one major bank cut **11 complaint systems to one**, others added automatic escalation when service levels were breached.

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: The FSCA's mandate includes promoting fair treatment; the six TCF outcomes describe what fair looks like across the customer journey.
Conduct Standard 3 of 2020 applies fair treatment rules to banks; this quest keeps its detail general because its text could not be opened.
Adverts must be clear, fair, factually correct and approved through a proper governance step; African Bank was penalised R700 000 in 2025.
The FSCA's 2025 review found no bank fully met the complaints rules assessed; keeping complainants informed was the weakest area.
Record, categorise, acknowledge, update, explain and point to the ombud: that is complaints handling the FSCA expects.

cards.prompt: Think of the last complaint you handled or heard about. Did the customer know who was dealing with it, how long it would take, why the decision was made and where to go next?

quiz.question: Which law gives the FSCA the objective of protecting financial customers by promoting their fair treatment?
options: The Banks Act
The Protected Disclosures Act
The Protection of Personal Information Act
The Financial Sector Regulation Act
quiz.explanation: Section 57 of the Financial Sector Regulation Act sets the FSCA's objectives, including protecting financial customers by promoting their fair treatment by financial institutions.

quiz.question: Which instrument is known as the Conduct Standard for Banks?
options: Board Notice 194 of 2017
Conduct Standard 3 of 2020
Joint Standard 2 of 2024
Directive 7 of 2022
quiz.explanation: The FSCA's Conduct Standard 3 of 2020 (Banks) is the Conduct Standard for Banks. BN 194 of 2017 is the FAIS fit and proper Determination.

quiz.question: A customer was promised his savings could be withdrawn at any time, but the product locks funds for 12 months. Which TCF outcome is mainly breached?
options: Products perform as customers were led to expect
Fair culture in the bank
Suitable product design for the target market
Complaints handled without barriers
quiz.explanation: Outcome 5 expects products to perform as customers were led to expect. Information failures (outcome 3) contributed, but the product does not do what he was told it would.

quiz.question: According to the FSCA's 2025 penalty decision, which part of the Conduct Standard for Banks did African Bank's advert contravene?
options: Section 8, on complaints
FAIS Act section 7, on authorisation
Section 6, on advertising
BN 194 section 13, on competence
quiz.explanation: The FSCA found breaches of section 6(1), 6(3)(a) and (b) on clear, fair and factually correct advertising, and 6(9) on the approval process.

quiz.question: What share of banks did the FSCA's 2025 review find kept complainants adequately informed of progress, delays and decisions?
quiz.explanation: 92% of banks did not comply with the requirement to keep complainants informed, so only 8% did. The 40% figure is the share that categorised complaints correctly.

quiz.question: Sipho rejects a complaint about a card fee. What should the response include, based on the section 8 requirements the FSCA assessed?
options: A short apology and the branch phone number
A referral to the police for a statement
A voucher in place of any explanation
Clear reasons, escalation options and the relevant ombud's details
quiz.explanation: When a complaint is rejected, the bank should give clear and adequate reasons, explain any escalation or review process and its time limits, and give the relevant ombud's contact details.

quiz.question: Why did the FSCA say correct categorisation of complaints matters?
options: It lets banks close complaints faster
It reduces the ombud's workload
It supports root cause analysis and prevents recurrence
It replaces the need to keep records
quiz.explanation: The FSCA recommended correct categorisation because it helps banks do robust root cause analysis and put measures in place to stop problems recurring.

quiz.question: In the African Bank case, why was R200 000 of the R700 000 penalty suspended?
options: The advert was found not to be misleading
Cooperation and prompt remedial action, subject to continued compliance
The bank appealed and won
The public figure paid that part instead
quiz.explanation: The FSCA took the nature of the contravention and the bank's remedial steps into account, suspending R200 000 for two years on condition that the bank stays fully compliant with the Conduct Standard.

quiz.question: Which practice did the FSCA's 2025 review criticise in how some banks handled complainants?
options: Referring them to the police instead of the ombud
Giving them the handler's contact details
Programming service levels into systems
Categorising complaints at closure
quiz.explanation: Some banks referred clients to SAPS for further help rather than giving them the relevant ombud's details. The other practices were noted as good practice.

quiz.question: At which stages did the FSCA expect banks to communicate the availability and contact details of the relevant ombud?
options: Only after a complaint is finally rejected
Only when the customer asks for them
Only in the bank's annual report
At all relevant stages, including point of sale and periodic communications
quiz.explanation: The review assessed section 8(23)(b), which expects ombud details at all relevant stages of the relationship, including point of sale, relevant periodic communications and when a complaint is rejected.

sessions.title: Speaking up, confidentiality and assessment readiness
sessions.summary: Use the Protected Disclosures Act and POPIA in practice, see how the bank's programme fits together and prepare honest evidence for the FSCA.
objectives: Explain what a protected disclosure is and the protection against occupational detriment
Apply the employer's duties, including internal procedures and the 21-day response
Protect customer information under POPIA's confidentiality and breach rules
Prepare honest evidence of competence and complaints handling for a regulator

cards.title: Stage five: what Lerato saw
cards.setting: Polokwane branch, after closing. Then a call to Sandton.

lines.text: Nandi, can I tell you something in confidence? A senior consultant here backdates suitability records after the sale. He says everyone does it to hit targets.
Thank you for telling me. You're doing exactly what the bank's speak-up procedure is for, and the law protects you for it.
He's my team leader's friend. What if they move me, or give me a bad review?
That's the fear that keeps most people quiet. The Protected Disclosures Act exists so it doesn't have to.
And while we look into it, those customer files are personal information. We protect them, even inside the investigation.
Final stage: speaking up, keeping information confidential, and proving the whole programme works. Then the final exam.

cards.title: The Protected Disclosures Act at work

scenes.heading: What a disclosure is
scenes.narration: Under the Protected Disclosures Act, a disclosure is information an employee or worker has reason to believe shows wrongdoing, such as a crime, a failure to meet a legal obligation, danger to health or safety, environmental damage, unfair discrimination, or the hiding of any of these.

scenes.heading: The employer's duty
scenes.narration: Since the 2017 amendments, every employer must authorise internal procedures for receiving and dealing with information about wrongdoing, and take reasonable steps to make every employee and worker aware of them.

scenes.heading: Protection
scenes.narration: An employee or worker who makes a protected disclosure may not be subjected to occupational detriment, such as dismissal, demotion, harassment, an unwanted transfer, a refused promotion or a bad reference.

scenes.heading: A response clock
scenes.narration: The person or body receiving a protected disclosure under the internal route must, within 21 days, decide whether to investigate or refer it and tell the discloser in writing, where their identity is known.

scenes.heading: Honesty both ways
scenes.narration: Protection is for genuine disclosures. Knowingly disclosing false information, intending to cause harm, is a criminal offence where harm results.

cards.title: Protected speaking up versus a damaging leak

items.label: Channel
items.left: The bank's authorised procedure, or a legal adviser
items.right: Social media or a forwarded file to an outsider

items.label: Good faith
items.left: Honest belief that wrongdoing is shown
items.right: Personal grudge or knowingly false claims

items.label: Customer data
items.left: Shared only as the procedure needs

items.label: Legal position
items.right: May lose protection; POPIA and offence risks

items.label: Outcome
items.right: Harm to customers and the case itself

cards.caption: The Act also protects some disclosures to bodies such as the Public Protector or the Auditor-General, and in limited cases wider disclosures. Your bank's procedure explains the routes.

cards.question: Lerato reports the backdating through Amanzi Bank's speak-up line in good faith. Her team leader then moves her to a branch two hours away against her will. Under the Protected Disclosures Act, what is that transfer?
options: A normal management decision
An occupational detriment
Allowed if her pay stays the same
Allowed if HR approves it
cards.explanation: Being transferred against one's will is listed as an occupational detriment. An employer may not subject an employee to occupational detriment on account, or partly on account, of a protected disclosure.

cards.title: POPIA confidentiality in everyday banking
cards.body:
The Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) applies to the bank as a **responsible party**. In general terms:

- The bank must secure the **integrity and confidentiality** of personal information with appropriate technical and organisational measures: identify risks, keep safeguards in place, check they work and update them.
- Anyone processing personal information on the bank's behalf must do so **only with its authorisation**, treat it as **confidential**, and not disclose it unless the law requires it or their proper duties need it.
- If there are reasonable grounds to believe personal information was **accessed or acquired by an unauthorised person**, the bank must notify the Information Regulator and the affected customers **as soon as reasonably possible**.
- An **information officer** must encourage and ensure the bank's compliance.

In practice: share only what a task needs, use approved channels, and report a suspected compromise at once through your bank's incident process.

cards.title: Speak up, keep confidential, or both?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation by what it mainly calls for.
buckets: Raise it through the speak-up procedure

items.text: A colleague backdates advice records to hide unsuitable sales
You must email a customer's ID copy to the complaints team
You find a manager selling customer lists to a lender
A friend asks whether her neighbour banks with Amanzi
A supervisor tells staff to stop logging complaints to improve figures
Evidence of misconduct includes customers' account statements
A team leader pressures staff to skip product training before a launch
A printout of customers' balances is left at the branch printer

cards.title: A turn: the inspection letter

lines.text: Team, the FSCA has written. It wants evidence of how we keep representatives competent and how we handle complaints.
Competence register, CPD records, training records within 15 days, reviews of each person. I can pull it all.
My register has gaps from last year. Some rejected complaints don't show the ombud details we gave.
And the backdating case? Do we have to hide it?
No. We show what we found, what we fixed and what we learned. Honest evidence beats a polished story every time.

cards.title: Preparing for the FSCA's request
cards.situation: The FSCA asks Amanzi Bank for evidence on representatives' competence and complaints handling. Pieter's records are strong, but the complaints register has gaps and an internal investigation into backdated advice records is still open. The deadline is two weeks away.

choices.text: Submit accurate records, explain the known gaps and the remediation plan with owners and dates, and disclose the open investigation as required, keeping customer data secure and shared only as needed.
